seo.title: Winter Day Tour from Seoul — Seoraksan, Nami Island & Eobi Valley Ice Wall

routeShapeIntro.title: How this winter day moves
routeShapeIntro.subtitle: A 06:00 Hongik / 06:30 Myeongdong start and a ~3-hour run northeast puts you at Seoraksan mid-morning, when the snow is still clean and the light is on the granite. Lunch near Sokcho, then the long drive back west through the Chuncheon corridor to Nami Island for the frosted tree avenues. The last stop, Eobi Valley, sits in southern Gapyeong already pointing at Seoul — you reach it late in the afternoon, near the end of the village's opening hours. Back in Seoul around 19:00-19:30.

routePhases.description: Pickup at 06:00 Hongik / 06:30 Myeongdong, then a ~3-hour drive northeast on the Seoul-Yangyang Expressway with one comfort stop, arriving at the Sogongwon entrance around 09:30.

Self-guided time at the Sogongwon entrance: the Tongildaebul bronze Buddha, Sinheungsa Temple, and the lower valley paths under snow. The cable car is not included and runs only when wind and ice allow.
Lunch near Sokcho (own expense), then the ~2-hour drive back west to Gapyeong Wharf and the five-minute ferry to Nami Island for two hours among the frosted metasequoia avenues.
Forty minutes south to Eobi Valley for the ice wall in late-afternoon light, then the ~1.5-hour run into Seoul — Myeongdong around 19:00, Hongik around 19:30.

bestFor: Travellers visiting Korea in January or February who want the winter landscape, not a city day
Photographers after snow on granite, frosted tree avenues and a blue-hour ice wall
Couples and small groups comfortable with a long, cold, full day
Anyone who wants to see something most Seoul day trips do not include
lessIdealFor: Anyone travelling outside the winter season — the ice wall simply does not exist in warm months
Travellers sensitive to cold, or who need guaranteed sightseeing regardless of weather
Guests wanting minimal walking — there is icy ground and a deck path at the last stop
Young children and anyone unsteady on their feet in winter conditions

items.label: Seoraksan first, while the snow is still clean
items.detail: The park is the furthest point of the day and the one most affected by afternoon melt and cloud. Going there first uses the clearest light and the freshest snow, and it means the long drive happens before anyone is tired.

items.label: Nami in the middle, because the ferry needs daylight
items.detail: Nami's appeal in winter is its tree avenues under frost, which need light to be worth the crossing. A mid-afternoon slot gets you across while the island is still bright and before the wind picks up on the exposed ferry deck.

items.label: Eobi last, because it is already on the way home
items.detail: Eobi Valley is in Seorak-myeon in southern Gapyeong, on the Seoul side of everything else on this route. Ending there costs no backtracking, and in deep winter the late arrival coincides with the valley's night lighting coming on along the deck path.

items.label: A route built around one short season
items.detail: The ice wall only exists when the cold holds — the village starts building it in mid-December and it comes down in February. That single constraint is why this itinerary exists at all and why it does not run the rest of the year.

seoraksanWhy: Seoraksan opens the day because it is both the furthest stop and the most light-dependent one. At 09:30 the snow on the granite ridges is still clean and the valley has not yet clouded over, which is the whole reason to drive three hours for it. Two hours at the Sogongwon entrance is enough for the Tongildaebul bronze Buddha, Sinheungsa Temple and the lower valley paths at a winter pace — not enough for a summit attempt, which is deliberate. Going first also gets the day's longest drive done before anyone is tired or cold.

seoraksanVisitBasics.hours: Park open year-round; Sinheungsa Temple from 06:00. The Gwongeumseong cable car runs in winter but its hours change daily with weather and it suspends in strong wind or ice — the operator posts each morning's schedule, so it is never guaranteed
seoraksanVisitBasics.closed: Open year-round, but high-altitude trails close seasonally for fire prevention and safety — typically from mid-November to mid-December and again from around mid-February. This itinerary uses only the low valley paths near the entrance, which are not affected
seoraksanVisitBasics.admission: Park entrance FREE (the ₩3,500 fee was abolished in May 2023). Cable car round-trip ₩16,000 adult, on-site ticketing only, NOT included in this tour and not guaranteed to run
seoraksanVisitBasics.walking: Easy to moderate on the valley floor — paved and stepped paths to Sinheungsa and the Tongildaebul, snowy and slippery in places. No hiking is scheduled; sturdy non-slip footwear is essential

seoraksanSmartNotes.photo: The Tongildaebul bronze Buddha against snow-dusted granite is the shot. In winter the Ulsanbawi ridge line is usually visible from the entrance plaza on clear mornings.
seoraksanSmartNotes.facilities: Visitor centre, cafes, restaurants and gift shops at the Sogongwon entrance. Indoor warm-up space is limited on busy winter days.
seoraksanSmartNotes.tip: Do not plan around the cable car. Winter hours shift daily and it closes on wind and ice more often than in other seasons; queues can also run long on clear days. Treat it as a bonus, not a fixture. Dress for −5 °C to +5 °C at the base with a strong wind chill.

namiWhy: Nami sits in the middle of the day because it is the one stop that needs both daylight and a boat. The metasequoia and ginkgo avenues under frost are what the island is worth crossing for in winter, and they need light; the ferry deck is also exposed, so a mid-afternoon crossing is more comfortable than a late one. Placing it after Seoraksan also breaks the long westward drive into two manageable legs rather than one.

namiVisitBasics.hours: Ferry from 08:00, last boat in at 21:00, roughly every 10-20 minutes through the day; most on-island shops close by 18:00. Winter schedules can change with weather
namiVisitBasics.admission: Naminara Republic visa fee, round-trip ferry included: Adult ₩19,000 — INCLUDED in this tour
namiVisitBasics.walking: Easy — flat tree-lined paths, though they can be icy underfoot in midwinter. The half-perimeter walk is ~3 km. Bicycle and e-buggy rental is available on the island at your own expense

eobi.name: Eobi Valley Ice Wall
eobi.description:
Eobi Valley — 어비계곡, from the characters for 'flying fish', after water that once ran fast enough to make fish look airborne — is a three-kilometre valley in Seorak-myeon, southern Gapyeong. In summer it is a swimming and trout stream. In winter it becomes something the rest of the year gives no hint of.

**The ice wall here is made, not found.** Since the winter of 2023 the residents of Garil 2-ri have sprayed water down the valley's rock face through the coldest weeks and let the cold do the rest, building it up into a sheet reported at around **25 metres** high. It is run by the village's own residents' association — roughly thirty people — as an off-season income project for a valley that previously had almost no winter visitors. You will see this described elsewhere, including on some official tourism pages, as a natural frozen waterfall. It is not, and it is more impressive for that.

Viewing is from a **wooden deck path** along the valley, part of a Gyeonggi Province restoration project that also added the night lighting. **The ground directly beneath the wall is closed off** after visitors were injured slipping there, so photographs are taken from the designated viewing area rather than from underneath. Alongside the wall the village runs an ice-sledding slope, a spinning snow sled, an igloo photo zone and a small heated greenhouse garden.

We arrive late in the afternoon, close to the end of the hours the village publishes for the festival ground. In deep winter that means the last of the daylight on the ice — good for photographs, and cold. The village does light the deck path in peak season, but the lighting comes on around the time it closes, so this itinerary does not promise it. Small fees are charged on site by the village for the viewing area and the sled activities; these are set locally and change year to year.
highlights: An ice wall reported at around 25 m, grown on the valley rock face by villagers of Garil 2-ri since winter 2023 — built, not natural
Run by the village residents' association (about 30 people) as an off-season project, branded 어비계곡 겨울나라, 'Eobi Valley Winter Wonderland'
Wooden deck viewing path with night lighting, added under Gyeonggi Province's clean-valley restoration scheme
Ice sledding, a spinning snow sled, an igloo photo zone and a heated greenhouse garden alongside the wall
The valley's name 어비 (魚飛) means 'flying fish' — from water once fast enough to make fish appear to fly
Visitor numbers roughly doubled to about 60,000 in a season as word spread, mostly among Southeast Asian travellers
timeUsed: Coach parks and the guide walks the group to the valley entrance (~10 min)
Deck path to the ice-wall viewing area and photographs (~25 min)
Optional sledding or greenhouse garden, or back to the coach early to warm up (~10 min)
eobi.whyOnRoute: Eobi closes the day for two reasons. Geographically it is the only stop on the Seoul side of the route — Seorak-myeon sits in southern Gapyeong, already pointing home — so an hour here costs no extra driving at the end of a long day. Editorially it is the reason this itinerary is a winter product rather than a year-round one: Seoraksan and Nami can be visited in any season, but the ice wall exists for perhaps eight weeks, and only if the cold holds. It is also the stop most travellers have never heard of, which is a good note to end on.

visitBasics.hours: Village-run and seasonal. The village publishes 10:00-17:00 for the festival ground (Eobi Valley Village, 031-585-3551). This itinerary arrives near the end of that window, so the paid activities may already be closing; the valley and its deck path are open ground rather than a gated site. Hours are set locally each year
visitBasics.closed: Winter only — provisionally mid-December to mid-February. The village sets the dates each year, so this is a guide rather than a published schedule: the 2025-26 season ran 20 December to 19 February, and the 2026-27 dates are not yet announced. The wall only appears once the cold holds; January and early February are the most reliable weeks
visitBasics.admission: Not included. The village charges about ₩1,000 per person for the ice-wall viewing area; sled and activity passes run roughly ₩5,000-30,000 on top. Parking at the village-entrance lot is free, and it is about a 500 m walk along the valley deck path to the festival ground. Fees are set locally and change year to year; the guide confirms the day's charges on the coach
visitBasics.walking: Short but genuinely icy. A mostly flat wooden deck path leads to the viewing area; the approach and surroundings are slippery and non-slip footwear is essential. The ground directly beneath the ice wall is closed to visitors. Not suitable for wheelchairs or strollers

smartNotes.photo: Shoot from the designated viewing area on the deck — under the wall is fenced off. Late afternoon gives you fading daylight on the ice and then the deck lighting; both work, and the transition between them is the best window.
smartNotes.facilities: Village-run and basic: a heated greenhouse garden, sled slope and small stalls. Do not count on substantial food or extensive indoor warm-up space.
smartNotes.tip: Wear non-slip winter footwear and treat the ice wall as weather-dependent rather than guaranteed — a warm spell shrinks it and the village decides its own opening. Bring small cash for the on-site fees.

pickup.name: Pickup (Hongik University Station or Myeongdong Station)
pickup.description:
Pickup is at one of two Seoul meeting points: **(1) Starbucks Hongik University Station Exit 8 (Mapo-gu)** at 06:00 — the Starbucks storefront sits immediately at the top of Exit 8; OR **(2) Myeongdong Station Exit 2 (Jung-gu)** at 06:30 — the NorthFace flagship store is the visible landmark next to the exit.

Both pickup points share the same heated coach and Hongik passengers board first. Please be at your chosen point **5 minutes before the scheduled time** — this is an early start on a cold morning and the day only works if the coach reaches Seoraksan by 09:30.

Dress for the whole day at boarding, not for the walk to the subway: you will be outdoors at −5 °C or colder at two of the three stops, and the last one is on ice. The guide distributes a printed Korean-English itinerary card and confirms the day's plan, including whether the Seoraksan cable car is running and what the village is charging at Eobi.
timeUsed: Arrive at your chosen pickup point 5 minutes before the scheduled time (~5 min)
Identify the AtoC Korea coach at the marked Starbucks / NorthFace frontage (~5 min)
Board in the pickup queue (~10 min)
Printed Korean-English itinerary card distributed at boarding
pickup.whyOnRoute: Two pickup points cover Seoul's two main visitor clusters — the Hongik University area in Mapo-gu and Myeongdong in Jung-gu — and Hongik first is the natural order for a northeast-bound run. The 06:00 start is not padding: Seoraksan is roughly three hours away and the value of going there in winter is being on the valley floor while the light is still on the snow. A later departure would put the park visit into the afternoon flatness and push the last stop past dark.

lunch.name: Lunch near Sokcho (own expense)
lunch.description:
The coach stops for about fifty minutes at a local restaurant near Seoraksan or on the Sokcho side after the park. Lunch is **not included** — you order and pay for what you want, typically ₩10,000-15,000 per person.

This is the east-coast seafood belt, so the local choices are things like **hoedeopbap** (raw fish over rice), grilled fish, or **sundubu jjigae** — the soft-tofu stew that Sokcho's Cheoksan district is known for and which is exactly the right thing to eat after two hours in the snow. Vegetarian options are limited; tell the guide in the morning and they will call ahead.

Bring cash or card. Fifty minutes is deliberately brisk — the drive back west to Nami is two hours and the last two stops both need daylight.
timeUsed: Coach parks and the guide walks the group to the restaurant (~5 min)
Pay individually and reassemble at the coach (~10 min)
lunch.whyOnRoute: Lunch sits directly after Seoraksan because it is the only point in the day where a proper sit-down stop does not cost daylight. Everything after it is time-sensitive: Nami needs light for the tree avenues, and Eobi needs to be reached before the village's viewing area closes. Eating here also means warming up straight after the coldest walking of the day.

dropoff.name: Return to Seoul (Myeongdong or Hongik University Station)
dropoff.description:
Departure from Eobi Valley is around 17:30 for the ~1.5-hour run into Seoul. Drop-offs are in reverse pickup order: **Myeongdong Station around 19:00**, then **Hongik University Station around 19:30**.

Both are subway interchanges. Winter conditions are the main variable on this leg — snow on the Gapyeong roads or Friday and Sunday evening traffic can add 30-60 minutes, and the guide will give the coach's live estimate on the way in. It is a long day; most guests sleep through this stretch.
timeUsed: Motorway drive into Seoul (~1.5 hours, longer in snow or weekend traffic)
dropoff.whyOnRoute: Ending at Eobi is what keeps the return short: the valley is already the closest stop to Seoul on this route, so the coach is pointed home from the moment it leaves. Reversing the drop-off order means Myeongdong guests, who boarded last, get out first.

Moderate, and the difficulty here is ice rather than distance or gradient.
Seoraksan: paved and stepped valley paths to Sinheungsa and the Tongildaebul, snowy and slippery in places. No hiking is scheduled and no summit is attempted.
Nami Island: flat paved tree-lined avenues, ~3 km over two hours, icy underfoot in midwinter.

lunch.title: Lunch (own expense)
content: Lunch is taken around 11:45 near Seoraksan or on the Sokcho side, straight after the park.
East-coast choices: hoedeopbap (raw fish over rice), grilled fish, or Sokcho's well-known sundubu jjigae soft-tofu stew.
Budget roughly ₩10,000-15,000 per person; cash and card are both normally accepted.
The stop is a brisk 50 minutes — the two remaining stops are time-sensitive. Vegetarian options are limited, so tell the guide in the morning.
This is a winter-season tour and weather is part of the product, not an exception to it.

**The Eobi ice wall is not guaranteed.** It is built by villagers over the coldest weeks and a warm spell shrinks or removes it. The village decides its own opening. If the wall is not viewable on your date we will tell you before departure and offer a rebooking or refund of that portion.
**The Seoraksan cable car is not guaranteed either.** Its hours change daily and it suspends in strong wind or ice. It is not included in the price, so nothing is lost if it does not run.

Heavy snow: the coach carries winter tyres and the tour normally still runs, but the return can take an extra hour. Severe snow or road closures can cancel the departure entirely — a full refund applies.
The Nami ferry can be suspended in severe weather; if that happens the guide extends the other stops and the Nami admission is refunded.

what-to-bring.title: What to wear & bring
content: **Non-slip winter footwear** — the single most important item. All three stops have ice underfoot.
Proper cold-weather layers: expect −5 °C or colder at Seoraksan with significant wind chill, and dusk temperatures at Eobi.
Gloves, hat and something covering your ears. The Nami ferry deck is fully exposed.
Small cash for Eobi's village-run fees and for lunch (₩10,000-15,000).
Camera or smartphone, plus a spare battery — cold drains batteries fast, and this is a route people photograph heavily.

practicalSeasonWindow.title: When this tour runs
content: This is a **winter-only** itinerary. It exists because the Eobi Valley ice wall exists, and that is a seasonal, village-built structure rather than a permanent attraction.
The wall typically begins forming from **mid-December** once the valley water freezes, and is most reliable through **January and early February**.
Season end varies year to year — the **2025-26 season closed on 19 February**. Dates for the coming winter are set by the village and confirmed at booking.
Outside the season, the same Seoraksan and Nami Island pairing is available year-round on our Seoraksan + Nami Island + Garden of Morning Calm day tour.

seasonalVariations.description: The ice wall starts to form once the valley water freezes hard. Early in the season it is smaller and the village may still be building it up. Seoraksan usually has its first settled snow.

The strongest month by a clear margin. The ice wall is at full height, Seoraksan's snow cover is most reliable, and Nami's tree avenues are properly frosted. Coldest temperatures of the year — dress accordingly.
Still dependable in most years, and marginally longer daylight at the Eobi stop. Watch for warm spells, which shrink the wall quickly.

The tour does not run. The ice wall is gone by late February and Eobi returns to being a summer swimming valley. For Seoraksan and Nami outside winter, see our Seoraksan + Nami Island + Garden of Morning Calm day tour.

staticQuestions.question: Is the Eobi ice wall natural?
staticQuestions.answer: No — and we would rather tell you than let you find out on the day. Since the winter of 2023 the residents of Garil 2-ri village have sprayed water down the valley's rock face through the coldest weeks and let it freeze into a sheet reported at around 25 metres high. You will see it described as a natural frozen waterfall on some tourism sites, including official English-language ones. That is incorrect. It is a village-built spectacle, run by about thirty local people as an off-season income project, and we think that is a better story than the one on the brochures.

staticQuestions.question: Is the ice wall guaranteed?
staticQuestions.answer: No, and any tour that guarantees it is overpromising. The wall depends on sustained cold and on the village's own decision to open — a warm spell shrinks it. If it is not viewable on your departure date we will tell you before you travel and offer a rebooking or a refund of that portion. It is most reliable in January and early February.

staticQuestions.question: When exactly does this tour run?
staticQuestions.answer: Winter only. The ice wall typically starts forming from mid-December and the 2025-26 season closed on 19 February. Exact dates are set each year by the village that builds the wall, so we confirm the running window at booking rather than publishing a fixed calendar we cannot keep.

staticQuestions.question: Is the Seoraksan cable car included?
staticQuestions.answer: No. The Gwongeumseong cable car costs ₩16,000 adult return, is sold on site only, and cannot be reserved in advance. In winter it matters more than usual that it is excluded: its operating hours change daily and it suspends in strong wind or ice, so it is genuinely not something we can promise. Park entrance itself is free and has been since May 2023.

staticQuestions.question: How cold does it actually get?
staticQuestions.answer: Cold enough that footwear and layers decide whether you enjoy the day. Expect roughly −5 °C to +5 °C at the Seoraksan valley floor with a strong wind chill, and colder in the shade. Nami's ferry deck is fully exposed. At Eobi you are standing still, at dusk, next to a wall of ice. Bring gloves, a hat and something over your ears.

staticQuestions.question: What footwear do I need?
staticQuestions.answer: Non-slip winter shoes or boots. This is the one piece of kit we would insist on. All three stops have ice underfoot — Seoraksan's stepped valley paths, Nami's flat avenues, and Eobi's deck path and approach. Ordinary trainers are not adequate. We do not require or provide crampons; the walking is short, it is the surface that is the issue.

staticQuestions.question: Is there much walking?
staticQuestions.answer: Not much distance — the difficulty is the surface, not the length. Seoraksan uses only the low valley paths near the entrance, with no hiking or summit attempt. Nami is flat, roughly 3 km over two hours if you walk the half-perimeter. Eobi is a short deck path. But all of it is icy, so allow more time and care than the distances suggest.

staticQuestions.question: Is this suitable for children or older travellers?
staticQuestions.answer: Less so than our other day trips, and we would steer you elsewhere if either applies strongly. It is a 13-hour day starting at 06:00, in deep-winter cold, with icy footing at every stop. The Eobi deck path is not suitable for strollers or wheelchairs, and the ground beneath the ice wall is fenced off. Children who enjoy snow and are properly dressed do fine; unsteady walkers will not.

staticQuestions.question: Are there fees to pay on the day?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes, two kinds. Lunch is your own expense at roughly ₩10,000-15,000. At Eobi the village charges small on-site fees — the ice-wall viewing area has been around ₩1,000 per person, with sledding extra. These are set locally and change year to year, so bring a little cash and the guide will confirm the day's amounts on the coach. Seoraksan park entry is free and the Nami ferry and admission are already included.

staticQuestions.question: Why do we arrive at Eobi so late in the day?
staticQuestions.answer: Because of where it is. Eobi Valley sits in southern Gapyeong, closer to Seoul than either Seoraksan or Nami, so visiting it last means the coach is already pointed home and the return stays short. In midwinter a 16:45 arrival means you see the last of the daylight on the ice and then the deck lighting coming on, which is a good window for photographs — but it is also the coldest part of the visit, so dress for standing still outdoors.

staticQuestions.question: How is this different from your other Seoraksan tours?
staticQuestions.answer: The third stop and the season. Our year-round Seoraksan day trip pairs the park with Nami Island and the Garden of Morning Calm — a gentler, garden-focused day that runs in any weather. This one swaps the garden for the Eobi ice wall and only exists while the wall does. If you are visiting outside January and February, the year-round route is the one you want.

staticQuestions.question: What happens if it snows heavily?
staticQuestions.answer: Usually the tour still runs — the coach carries winter tyres in season and snow is rather the point. Expect the return leg to take up to an hour longer. If snowfall is severe enough to close roads we cancel the departure and refund in full. We would rather cancel than run a 13-hour mountain day in unsafe conditions.
